# Voice profile — eff-mullin

> Confidence: full — 11 usable samples, 8,066 words. Voice card empty; all observations are derived from the corpus.

## 1. Cadence

Sentences run middle-length most of the time, with short declaratives placed for emphasis. The short sentence comes at the end of a paragraph or stands alone as its own paragraph, carrying the verdict. After two or three clauses that explain a mechanism or describe a risk, let the next sentence be six words and flat — 9/11 samples, several times per piece.

`kids-online-safety-act-will-make-internet-worse-everyone`: *"When the safest legal option is to delete a forum, platforms will delete the forum."* `why-are-gay-bars-building-databases-their-patrons`: *"This was not simply checking IDs at the door. PatronScan was building a database."* `court-records-should-be-free`: *"Public access to the courts is a cornerstone of democratic accountability."* — that last sentence appears twice in the same piece, once near the open and once at the close.

Longer sentences carry procedural explanation; shorter ones carry the judgment. You can usually tell which a paragraph is doing from its final sentence.

## 2. How a piece opens

Eight of eleven pieces follow a three-part opening shape: name the bill or issue, state its claimed purpose, immediately qualify or rebut — 8/11 samples.

`californias-ab-412-bill-could-crush-startups-and-cement-big-tech-ai-monopoly`: *"California legislators have begun debating a bill (A.B. 412) that would require AI developers to track and disclose every registered copyrighted work used in AI training. At first glance, this might sound like a reasonable step toward transparency. But it's an impossible standard..."*

`kids-online-safety-act-will-make-internet-worse-everyone`: *"The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA) is back in the Senate. Sponsors are claiming—again—that the latest version won't censor online content. It isn't true."*

The rebuttal arrives in the second or third sentence; the bill's own framing is never extended for a full paragraph before it is turned. The three remaining openings skip the concession entirely and open directly on the judgment: `california-ab-412-stalls-out-win-innovation-and-fair-use`: *"A.B. 412, the flawed California bill that threatened small developers..."*

## 3. How a piece closes

Nine of eleven pieces close with a direct instruction to the legislature, a coalition statement, or a reader call to action — 9/11 samples. The instruction is short, usually a pair of sentences. `congress-just-rushed-through-disastrous-copyright-office-overhaul`: *"The Senate should reject H.R. 6028. The Copyright Office should serve the public—not presidential administrations, and not industry lobbyists."* `kids-online-safety-act-will-make-internet-worse-everyone`: *"Lawmakers should reject it, and fast."* Two pieces close with a direct reader link to contact legislators. When a piece closes by naming what should happen, the final sentence names who should act and what they should do — no hedge, no question.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The prose speaks as EFF, not as an individual. The dominant pronoun is institutional *we*: [measurement:first-person-plural-family] Count case-sensitive whole-word tokens we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours, and the listed contracted we forms in the extracted sample bodies; uppercase US is excluded — 19 instances, 2.36 per 1,000 words, 10/11 samples, several times per piece. This *we* refers to EFF and its coalition partners; it never folds the reader in.

First-person singular is near-absent: [measurement:first-person-singular-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens I, me, my, mine, and myself in the extracted sample bodies — 2 instances, 0.25 per 1,000 words, established across all 11 samples. The writer does not appear as a person. Do not reach for *I*.

Second-person is sparse and purposeful: [measurement:second-person-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, and you'll in the extracted sample bodies — 11 instances, 1.36 per 1,000 words, 5/11 samples, once or twice per piece when present. It appears almost exclusively in direct calls to action (*"If you are a California resident..."*). Keep *you* out of the argument itself.

Contractions run throughout: [measurement:contractions] Count whole-word n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, and 'm forms plus 's only for the closed elision hosts it, that, there, here, who, what, where, when, how, why, he, she, let, one, nothing, everything, something, somebody, nobody, and this; possessive 's is excluded — 86 instances, 10.66 per 1,000 words, all 11 samples. Uncontracted negatives coexist with them throughout: [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] Count case-insensitive whole phrases do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, and had not in the extracted sample bodies — 32 instances, 3.97 per 1,000 words, 9/11 samples. Neither form is reserved for formal emphasis; use both freely.

Direct questions are sparse: [measurement:question-marks] Count every literal question-mark character in the extracted sample bodies — 9 instances, 1.12 per 1,000 words, 4/11 samples, once or twice per piece when present. Questions are rhetorical — they introduce a scenario the prose then unpacks: `kids-act-would-require-age-checks-get-online`: *"Can teens discuss addiction and recovery?"*

## 5. Figures

Figures are drawn from legal and procedural vocabulary — 9/11 samples. Comparisons reach for established legal mechanism or precedent: AI training compared to how search engines index images, a compliance obligation called *a death sentence* for a small startup, the copyright registration system described as *"more like a card catalog than a database."* Borrowed policy idioms recur: *a heckler's veto, sleight-of-hand, a solution in search of a problem* — 6/11 samples, once or twice per piece when present. These carry established meaning in policy debates; the prose imports rather than coins them. No rate is possible because I cannot draw a reliable boundary around "a figure" — this is a description of the vocabulary they are built from, not a count of figures.

## 6. Register range

All eleven samples occupy the same register: analytical advocacy, measured in tone, addressed to a policy-literate general audience. No sample shifts into humor, personal anecdote, or polemic invective. The `why-are-gay-bars` piece spends more time on documented facts before moving to the policy argument; `court-records-should-be-free` is brief and close to a statement of support rather than a full analysis. Neither is a different voice.

Parenthetical spans are the main structural mechanism for managing complexity: [measurement:round-parenthetical-spans] Count each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line in the extracted sample bodies — 97 instances, 12.03 per 1,000 words, all 11 samples, throughout. They carry acronym expansions, bill citations, caveats, and supporting facts. Em-dashes serve a different function — interruption and intensification: [measurement:em-dashes] Count every literal em-dash character in the extracted sample bodies — 53 instances, 6.57 per 1,000 words, 10/11 samples, several times per piece. Parentheses add; em-dashes interrupt or sharpen.

Seven of eleven pieces use bold intra-prose section headings for each major point — 7/11 samples. The four shorter pieces omit them. Headings name the argumentative claim (*"A Burden That Small Developers Can't Bear," "This Bill Was Rushed Through"*), not the topic.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Profanity is absent from the entire corpus: [measurement:profanity-vulgarity] Count only the case-insensitive whole-word profanity and vulgarity forms enumerated by the prose-author corpus-rates profanity rule; coined words containing a rude root are excluded — 0 instances, 0 per 1,000 words, 0/11 samples. The rhetorical punch that profanity might deliver elsewhere is carried here by em-dashes and short declarative sentences: [measurement:em-dashes] 53 instances, 6.57 per 1,000 words, 10/11 samples. Against those 53 em-dashes, there are 0 profanity instances in the whole corpus. Use the em-dash and the short declarative for emphasis; do not introduce vulgarity.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

The corpus shows hedging (*"it's not at all clear," "could be read to also apply," "may simply forgo"*) but without a stable form — sometimes a modal, sometimes an adverb, sometimes a passive construction — and not consistently enough to produce an instruction.

Named opponents (*Big Tech* as a collective epithet, specific companies like Apple and X) and named coalition partners both appear, but the point at which they are introduced and how they are framed varies across pieces. No stable rule follows.

The corpus provides no evidence of how this voice behaves when supporting rather than opposing legislation. All eleven pieces oppose or raise alarms about a bill; `court-records-should-be-free` is the closest to an endorsement and is the shortest piece in the corpus.

4 observations were dropped for insufficient cross-sample support or inability to cite.
